title: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Jazz Number to Open ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2: ‘Hoping You’ll Like Me More Than Nando’s or Marmite’
description: Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in L
body:
Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in London. 

	“Can you believe this is Saturday night, first of all?” Goldblum asked the live audience after making his grand entrance. “And me, I’m hosting this gosh darn ‘SNL U.K.’ triumphant second season first episode! So, for the occasion, may we perform something we’ve just composed special for you tonight?”
	

	Goldblum, who has his own jazz band in addition to starring in franchises like “Wicked” and “Jurassic Park,” then took a seat behind the piano and began to sing a tune chock-full of U.K. references. “I’m hoping to be your precise cup of tea and that you’ll like me more than Nando’s or Marmite,” Goldblum sang. “Even if I still bomb, I will keep calm and carry on because I’m hosting from London tonight.”


	Goldblum danced around the stage and even made a reference to his “Wicked” role, singing: “Despite a few wicked flaws, I am the Wizard of Oz!”

	Musical guest CMAT then came out to help Goldblum with the lyrics, holding cue cards that read “Life Finds a Way,” in reference to his famous “Jurassic Park” line. “I don’t recognize it,” Goldblum said — but then the band begin to play the “Jurassic Park” theme and he remembered who he was. “I get it now, I can do it!” 

	“Life finds a way, when you’re live on Saturday,” he concluded with a big finish. “Like Sainsbury’s Local, we’re all feeling vocal. And I’m hosting right here, in London tonight!”

schema.headline: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Jazz Number to Open ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2: ‘Hoping You’ll Like Me More Than Nando’s or Marmite’

title: Camera-Shy Chrissie Hynde on Finally Allowing a Definitive Doc to Be Made About ‘The Pretenders,’ Bowing in Toronto: ‘I Just Wanted to Be in a Band. I’ve Never Graduated Beyond That Initial Interest in It’
description: At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on
body:
At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on film until “The Pretenders,” a Joss Crowley-directed doc that premieres Sunday at the Toronto International Film Festival. The band released what might rightly be considered the best rock ‘n’ roll debut album of all time in Janauary 1980, and Crowley’s film covers the lead-up to that — Chrissie Hynde looking and acting like a biker chick in late ’70s Akron before moving to and finding her real gang in the U.K. — and the tumultuous few years that followed, with further masterpieces arriving alongside band dismisals and deaths. Although the focus is on the original lineup and the first five years, it brings us into the present day of Hynde, still one of the greatest to ever pick up a guitar.

	As delightfully plain-spoken as Hynde is when you get her to sit down and talk, she can be to get into that chair, as a naturally camera-shy personality, so Crowley’s film is particularly useful in further immortalizing a subject who never wanted to be anything more than an ordinary musician, whether “rock goddess” was quickly and eternally thrust upon her or not.

	Variety spoke with Crowley and the delightfully tart-as-ever Hynde in advance of the Toronto premiere.

	Most of the time with modern music documentaries, it’s the artist or their company instigating the doc, and usually co-producing it. But it sounds like that’s not necessarily what happened this time because, Joss, you’ve talked about the difficulty in talking Chrissie into it.

	Joss Crowley: I’ve been trying to work with Chrissie and tell the Pretenders’ story for over 10 years, and kept knocking at the door; didn’t get an answer. It was just a question of right time, right place, and Chrissie came round to the idea of meeting me. We sat down and talked about some of the docs I’ve made, and about other things, trying to find some mutual interests. I wasn’t really sure when I left that meeting how it had gone, but within about a week, we sat down and recorded our first interview, at the end of 2023.

	Chrissie, you needed less than a week to think about it and get underway after that first meeting?

	Chrissie Hynde: Well, we had to have a go and see how it would go, and I think I must have laid down some sort of ground rules, so I was willing to go into it — that it would be (visually focused on) archive footage, and really talk about the band and not focus too much on me, and it wouldn’t be about “women in rock” or any of that kind of thing. It would just be a story of the band. I was kind of keen to have it done because, as we all know, there’s documentaries on everything and everyone now. And in fact, someone else had already made a documentary on the Pretenders, which had nothing to do with me or my entire organization. I was starting to get calls from some of my old friends saying, “Oh, I’m gonna do your documentary on Tuesday.” And I’d be like, “We’re not doing a documentary!” This other team had gone in to people I know and made it sound like it was an official documentary. So I thought, “Well, if that’s happened once, that’s gonna happen again.” Either you want to do it and you want your story out, or you don’t, which I didn’t particularly, but if it’s going to be out, I’d rather know that it’s true.



	

					Chrissie Hynde in ‘The Pretenders’
									Courtesy TIFF
	



	At the very end of the film, you’re heard talking a little bit about why you did it and you mention that you especially wanted to do it for James Honeyman-Scott [who suddenly died at the height of the band’s success in 1981], in some way.

	Hynde: For me, a rock band is all about electric guitar, and I think he was one of the great guitar heroes. Over the years when I see lists of the greatest 100 rock guitar players, I never see Jimmy’s name. That’s all he was interested in, music and playing the guitar, and I thought he didn’t get his due and that would be important for him. He’s not here, so I thought I could do it for him.

	It feels like the way the documentary turned out was kind a nice compromise in the end, since you didn’t want to be on-camera at all, but you were talked into being seen for the very last interview, so there’s a little bit but not a lot. You acquiesced a little bit.

	Hynde: Yeah. I haven’t seen it, and I probably won’t. Someone said, “Oh, don’t say that! That sounds negative.” But I think a lot of people don’t like watching themself or listening to themself talk, and I don’t have to watch it, and there you go. It’s not negative. I mean, I’ve already lived through it, so I don’t think I wanna go through it all again.


	I think so many people feel this way, and most people that I’ve ever had a conversation about it with do: they don’t like the sound of their speaking voice. I mean, I’ve had to get used to my singing voice because, you know, that’s kind of my shtick. But my speaking voice, when I hear it back, I’m always pretty horrified. And everyone I talk to feels the same way… People expect if you do it for a living, that you must like it, but that’s not necessarily true.


	One of your quotes in here is, “I like being in a band, I just don’t like being observed. It’s a real problem.” A lot of people will relate to that, wanting to have a voice — figuratively — while not liking the attention that comes with it.
	

	Hynde: I think so, because I think I represent just ordinary people, and that’s how I feel and that’s how I go through my life. You know, I get the public transport. I don’t live in a gated community. I’m just exactly the same way I always was, and I don’t want that taken away from me. I like hanging out. I’d rather sit on a doorstep and eat a slice of pizza than go to a fancy restaurant. I’ve always been like that, but I think most people are.


	It has become more common in documentaries to have the subjects entirely off-screen. I was recently watching Paul McCartney’s Wings documentary, and his interviews in it are all audio-only, which is great most of the time. But at the same time you’re kind of like, “Well, just show him to me for 10 seconds.”

	Hynde: Are you talking about “Man on the Run”? I loved that. In fact, I watched it sitting next to Paul when it was screening. He was singing along! I guess he’s so used to seeing himself. It was very moving for me to see Linda in the early days, even before I met her, and how cool and how beautiful she was… We’ve seen so many documentaries, it’s a matter of kind of getting away from the format. But, certainly, archive footage — we were lucky to have any for ours, because this was way before people had camera phones or were thinking much about taking photos.
	

	Crowley: There was a big archive breakthrough when we found this cameraman, Andy Watt, who’s from Hereford, like the band really, and he joined the original band on tour about three months before Pete left and Jimmy died. [Bassist Pete Farndon was dismissed in1982 and died the following year; Honeyman-Scott died two days after Frandon’s firing.] He was able to document two weeks on the road in North America with the band, and that footage has never been seen. We found all 20 tapes of it, and they were in very poor condition and pretty much unusable, but fortunately we found a retired engineer who was able to bring them back to life. Another thing that really helped the device was doing the interviews with Stan, the old tour manager, who read his diaries aloud, and we could suddenly see Jimmy and Pete in and around the band in the period where we focused the story, which is those five years between the end of the ’70s and the early ’80s.

	You start the movie with Stan Tippins, now an elder gent, reading these diaries for the camera. It seems like his participatino was really, no pun intended, a tipping point.

	Hynde: I’d love to see that stuff, with the Stan diaries. All the time that we were with Stan, he often mentioned, “Now I’m gonna go write my diary,” but no one ever saw them. Joss and I had dinner with Stan and Lynne Honeyman-Scott, Jimmy’s sister, and (original drummer) Martin Chambers, and it never even occurred to me that Stan would be willing to be actually filmed, reading his diaries. I’m dying to see all that part, so maybe I will have to watch it at some point. Stan was so important in the early band. He was our scout leader or something. We were new at this, and he had been a singer in Mott the Hoople [prior to Ian Hunter]. We loved him, because was like having a farmer in a band. He would say things like, “I don’t know why you would wanna take drugs when you could have a nice, juicy pear.” I suppose you could say we were laughing behind his back, but he was the wise man of the operation.

	When it came to your interviews, Chrissie, there ae some topics that are tricky or touchy, inevitably. It’s clear on camera when you are willing to get into something and when you aren’t. Joss asks you about Ray Davies, and you say, “I’d rather not get into it. There’s a lawsuit waiting to happen.” But it’s cool that we at least see you address not wanting to discuss something, whereas a lot of docs would just leave that out. And then, of course, you do get into a lot of tough stuff with the early ’80s with everything that happened with the band. Was it cathartic in any way to talk about the hard times of the band, or is it always just difficult?

	Hynde: First of all, talking about, for example, Ray Davies — I mean, anything with him or with anyone in my family — I don’t think it’s right to talk about other people because it’s an invasion of their privacy. I’ve never done that, and I don’t think that’s a very dignified thing to do. If people ask me, “Oh, are your kids musical?” I say, “Well, if you ever meet them, you ask them. I don’t wanna talk about it.” Not because I don’t love them, but because this is kind of an invasion of their privacy. And I’ve never talked to any journalist and given a list of things that they’re not allowed to ask. Because if I don’t wanna talk about it, then I can say, “Let’s not talk about it.” But not for any other reason than that. Because certainly as a Kinks fan, I mean, who doesn’t wanna talk about Ray Davies? He’s fucking amazing. But I just don’t do that.
	

	I can’t remember what Joss asked me about the grisly stuff in the ’80s, because I haven’t revisited that. But the other thing is, when you have a story that’s in public or when you become famous or whatever, your story isn’t that much more interesting than just an ordinary person’s. I mean, nobody hasn’t had bereavements and fuck-ups and disappointments and victories, and all these things that happen in a person’s life. I think there’s too much emphasis on the extraordinary life of celebrities.

	You’ve been clear from the beginning of your career up till now that you never wanted to be a poster girl or an emblem or spokesperson for anything.

	Hynde: Being in a rock band… I mean, who didn’t wanna be in a rock band? Did you wanna be in a rock band?

	Of course.

	Hynde: Are you now?

	No, sadly.

	Hynde: But you wanted to be. So, I’ve offered some music, and that’s all I’m offering. Everyone that I grew up with wanted to be in a rock band. That was my generation. We were all very ordinary kids. People didn’t get into bands to become celebrities. They just wanted to be in a band. I’ve never graduated beyond that initial interest in it.
	

	Surely you’ve grown in a thousand ways since the band’s early days, but the film kind of presents you as somebody who sort of had either a certain idealism or just a basic attitude about certain things and stuck to it.

	Hynde: I also had some great people that I’ve met in my life who were inspirational. Lemmy never changed. Lemmy was always the same. and that’s kind of been my motto. That’s why I don’t do fashion magazines. Well, there’s many reasons I don’t! But I always think, “Well, if you wouldn’t ask Lemmy to do it, don’t ask me.” Because he’s kind of, I suppose you could say, my style icon, if there is such a thing in the case of someone who was in Motörhead.

	Neil Young’s another. He’s never changed. You might not have ever met him, but anyone who’s listened to his music, you have met him. He’s exactly what you think he’s going to be. Bob Dylan, I mean, ia obviously more of an enigma, because he’s a little bit more of a trickster and a comedian. But he offered the world all that music and I’m not sure that he got into it to be the spokesman of his generation, which was the mantle that he had to carry. And in the case of Willie Nelson, Neil Young, Bob… First name basis, did you get that? [Laughs.] Paul McCartney’s the best example because he was in the fucking Beatles, and yet he’s still doing exactly what he was doing. If his band hadn’t made it that big, I reckon if he was still in Liverpool and he got married and had some kids, he’d probably still be playing in a band in a local bar somewhere, because that’s what he likes.

	Joss, is there any way to put in a nutshell what you wanted to capture about Chrissie in this film? And did it change at all as you spent so many hours with her?
	

	Crowley: To answer the first question, it’s the story of the Pretenders, which I know is obviously very much about Chrissie, but also about the rest of the band. But with Chrissie, I because I spent so many hours with her, I just wanted to make sure her personality came across in the film. Because I think that’s what documentary does perhaps better than any other medium, is that it brings personality to the screen. And so if it felt awkward at times, that’s OK. When it was successful, great. When the band was successful, great. And everything in between, and when it was emotional and sad, it had to be there. We were talking about voices earlier on, and I’ve had to get used to hearing my voice a bit because it was important to hear questions that I put to Chrissie that she didn’t want to answer, or at least didn’t want to answer initially and then came round to answering later on. Because that, I think, tells you as much about Chrissie as a perfectly articulated answer. So that was something I guess I warmed up to, the idea of keeping my questions in, which I haven’t done in previous documentaries. That was a good way to unlocking a bit more about who Chrissie is.

	The other question: in terms of hours, we would meet monthly, for a few hours…

	Hynde: Seems like most of my life. No, Joss did prompt me, but mainly I just imagined a certain time, an event that happened, and I would just talk about it for an hour, and then have a few cups of tea and leave. And then he’d have to figure it out. Definitely the early sessions were much more like that, and as it evolved, it became a bit more interview-based, I suppose, and it had a different rhythm to it.

	I didn’t want to ask my mates to sit down in front of a camera, because I find it uncomfortable, so I thought, “Well, why would I expect them to do it?” So I made a real point of just having talk over {i.e., audio-only interview]. But then you have to think about, if you’re on stage, what are you prepared to do? But then you also have to think about the audience: What do they want? And I’ve been in the audience as much as I’ve been on stage, if not more. I know the audience wants a certain thing. And [for a documentary] I know the audience wants to see people sitting down talking to camera. I know I want to see that.

	Crowley: There were two things that Chrissie said to me early on in the process. She said, “Make it good, and make it different.” And I think we’ve achieved that. But you can’t make something different for the sake of it being different. It has to work for the story that the film tells. And Chrissie doesn’t like cameras. Chrissie doesn’t like having her photograph taken. It was really hard to find archive as well because lots of times cameramen or camera crews weren’t allowed access to the band. It was hard on a lot of levels. So the fact that I managed to to convince Chrissie to go on camera for the final interview, it just sort of works. I think it’s an achievement of the film and also a reflection of how much she doesn’t want to be on camera all the time.

	You probably did get much more intimate stuff by allowing her to just speak into a microphone. And we get to luxuriate in the sound of her voice as she’s digging deep on some of that stuff…

	Hynde: Oh, God, when you said “luxuriate in the sound of her voice,” I’m cringing.

	You often say you don’t like to be a symbol of anything, but is anything you represent to the public that you kind of allow for yourself as being OK?

	Hynde: Well, of course I like being a sex symbol, but…

	Glad you brought that up, because that was something that struck me watching the movie — that to some people you were and are a sex symbol, and at the same time, there is Shirley Manson talking about how what you got out of it was loving seeing you be androgynous, so…
	

	Hynde: I was being facetious! [About being a sex symbol.] I’m just, you know… I’m a man of the people.

	One thing that hasn’t changed that you represent: being against rock turning completely consumerist. Every time I see a music star doing a product commercial, I think of your song “How Much Did You Get for Your Soul?”

	Hynde: Yeah. They’re all at it, aren’t they? Well, you know, fuck ’em.

	Joss, do you have a favorite moment in the movie?
	

	Crowley: Favorite part of the production of making the film, I guess, was when Stan opened his diaries for the first time, and he found the first time he met Chrissie in rehearsals, because it was such a breakthrough for me. I think he summed up quite a lot about, about Chrissie and the band in a few words. Do you know the bit I’m talking about? I can’t remember exactly what he says, but it’s something like, “She has quite a lot of fun, but underneath she might be a bit nervous.”

	Hynde: Oh, God, I hate to think what’s in those diaries. Fuck me. But we love Stan, so there you go.

	Chrissie, we can’t ask you if you have a favorite moment in the movie…

	Hynde: I saw my manager, Ian Grenfell, yesterday and I said, “Hey, is this gonna come across really negative if I say I haven’t watched it?” And he goes, “Don’t worry about it, because that horse has bolted. People already know [to expect] you haven’t watched it. And a lot of people do not watch their documentaries.” So I was relieved that I don’t have to tough it out… I’ve been very inspired in the last couple of days, seeing Noel and Liam (Gallagher, from Oasis) out there. They’ve got a documentary out and they’re on the front line going for it. But I just don’t have that kind of drive.

	I’m sure you’ll be in Toronto, Joss. Are you going, Chrissie, or will you be avoiding the premiere?

	Hynde: Yeah, I am going. And then Martin’s going. It’s gonna be me and Martin there on the red carpet, so that should be… Well, it won’t be a beauty contest.

schema.headline: Camera-Shy Chrissie Hynde on Finally Allowing a Definitive Doc to Be Made About ‘The Pretenders,’ Bowing in Toronto: ‘I Just Wanted to Be in a Band. I’ve Never Graduated Beyond That Initial Interest in It’

title: Celine Dion Delivers Tearful Speech on Opening Night of Paris Residency: ‘I Had Promised Myself Not to Cry’
description: Celine Dion shed tears as she kicked off her eagerly anticipated 16-date residency tonight at Plenitude Arena on the outskirts of Paris, marking her
body:
Celine Dion shed tears as she kicked off her eagerly anticipated 16-date residency tonight at Plenitude Arena on the outskirts of Paris, marking her first major series of live shows since stepping away from the spotlight in 2022.

	“I had promised myself not to cry,” Dion told thousands of adoring fans in the opening moments of her show. “I don’t keep my promises. But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you. I’m going to sing like you without crying.”
	

	She later added, “Thank you so very much for coming. If it’s your first time in Paris, I hope you fall in love with it just like I did. Finally, it’s amazing we are all together. I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. So here I am, singing for you and singing for me, singing live! Thank you so very much for your support, your patience and if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me.”


	Speaking of the uphill battle she waged with her health, Dion said, “By living with it day in and day out, I’ve come to terms with it. And I’ve decided to make it my reason for living.”

	She continued, “But look around here—all around you, right here in this room—we don’t know what the person next to us is going through. There are people going through hardships, grief, and sorrow. There are people radiating energy and joy. So let’s take that energy and share it. That’s what music is for. Tonight, we’ll sing, we’ll dance, and we’ll celebrate.”

	During her final words of the night, Dion told the audience, “Thank you so much. I just fulfilled a dream.” 

	Dion’s arrival in Paris two weeks ago has dominated headlines and sparked a frenzy on social media as well as in the streets of the French capital. The metro station near the concert venue has also been renamed Celine and has been decorated with some of her most famous lyrics. Fans from every corner of the world have been camping in front of the Royal Monceau hotel behind security barriers and have been singing her more popular songs every time she comes out. Clips of Dion engaging with fans, singing a cappella with them and making some dance moves in front of the Parisian palace have gone viral.
	

	Not all of those hardcore fans will make it to the Paris concerts, however. Some may be turned away if they unknowingly bought fake tickets from the more than 200 fraudulent websites and social media accounts that popped up right when presale tickets went on sale in April, according to the Associated Press, which quoted Group-IB, a Singapore-based cybersecurity firm.

	Her comeback isn’t just being eagerly anticipated by fans — it’s also being touted as a potential lifeline for France’s state coffers heading into 2027. French newspaper Liberation dedicated the cover of its weekend edition to Dion’s residency with a picture of the singer doing a prayerlike gesture, looking upward with a bright halo of light behind her and a headline that reads, “Celine Dion — is she going to save the 2027 budget?” Her Paris concerts could indeed generate €1 billion in economic impact for France, that’s four times more than what Beyoncé’s Paris concerts in June 2025 brought and roughly a fifth of what the entire Paris 2024 Olympics generated, according to French radio Europe 1.

	More than 33,000 people are expected at the Plenitude Arena. As much as 60% of the set list is expected to be from her French repertoire, mainly songs penned and composed by Jean-Jacques Goldman, including “Pour que tu m’aimes encore” and “J’irai où tu iras.” She’s also teased that her first show will last over two hours in an informal chat with fans in front of her hotel and told them to wear comfortable shoes, as reported by France Info.

	Rumors have been circulating about a potential surprise duo with Beyoncé who happens to be in the French capital with Jay-Z, who gave a concert in Paris two days ago.

	An estimated nine million people signed up for advance tickets for the shows after Dion announced her concert comeback on her birthday, on March 30, during a glamorous bash (which she didn’t attend but delivered a message on video) in front of the Eiffel Tower, which was illuminated in tribute, with a choreographed light show set to Dion’s greatest hits.

	Dion made her stage return singing Edith Piaf’s “Hymne A L’Amour” by the Eiffel Tower at the 2024 Paris Olympics opening ceremony.

	Dion’s Paris concerts were originally scheduled for 2020 at Paris La Defense Arena as part of her Courage World Tour, but were postponed due to the pandemic and then delayed again due to her health issues. In 2022, Dion was diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS), a rare neurological and autoimmune disorder that causes muscular stiffness, inhibiting the ability to walk and sing. Her fans lost hope she would ever come back after seeing Dion struggle against this illness in the 2024 documentary “I Am: Celine Dion,” which was directed by Irene Taylor.

schema.headline: Celine Dion Delivers Tearful Speech on Opening Night of Paris Residency: ‘I Had Promised Myself Not to Cry’

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s British Return in Cold Open: ‘Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!’
description: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U
body:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2.

	The cold open began with Larry Dean as King Charles II and Emma Sidi as Queen Camilla relaxing at Balmoral Castle in Scotland (“I do love our weekends away. No responsibilities, just like every other day,” says Camilla.)


	They are then interrupted by the arrival of Harry (Jack Shep) and Meghan (Ayoade Bamgboye). With much of the skit consisting of them being in a close embrace — to the disgust of King Charles — there were countless one-liners making fun of their decision to return to the U.K.
	

	“What do you two want?” asked an infuriated Charles. “Don’t tell me you’ve spent that Netflix money already.”


	“Daddy, it was $16 million,” replied Harry. “How long was it supposed to last?”

	“What a waste you’ve become, you’re lucky your father is not around to see this,” Charles responded, a line which received a large reaction in the room.

	Meghan’s lifestyle brands were also riffed on, with her presenting an ice tray to Camilla. “I made it myself,” she said. “I can give you the recipe. I’m a whizz in the kitchen.”

	“She hires the best chefs,” Harry added.

	George Fouracres, who received acclaim for his acute portrayal of former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, also made his first appearance as Prime Minister Andy Burnham, wearing his trademark black rimmed glasses. 

	“I’m the new PM. And I’m nothing like the last one,” he said. Making fun of Burnham’s raft of policies over the summer and his attempts at being relatable despite being in high office, the skit ended up with him saying: “I will buy everybody a pint, because I want you to like me. I need you to like me.”
	

	The first episode of “SNL U.K.” was hosted by Jeff Goldblum, who performed a jazzy number about spending time in London during his monologue.

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s British Return in Cold Open: ‘Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!’

title: Mia Wasikowska Fills Out the Screen As ‘Agata the Writer’ in Kuba Dorabialski’s Venice Drama: ‘It’s Our Responsibility to Understand Each Other’
description: Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence
body:
Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence shows her in close-up looking directly at the audience and recounting the rest of the story.  

	“I was so curious about it,” she says.  

	“Luckily, when I’m doing something, I don’t think too much about how it’s going to be perceived. Kuba sent me some references, which I thought were really interesting, and it felt organic. But then, when I was watching the scene, I thought: ‘Ok. That’s enough of my face’!”
	

	Known for blockbusters like “Alice in Wonderland” and high-profiles dramas “Stoker” or “Jane Eyre,” Wasikowska has been pursuing arthouse fare in recent years. 

	“I was really excited about making a film that didn’t follow a typical narrative structure. I feel like we have tunnel vision about how to tell a story and make a film,” notes Wasikowska. She also executive produced the film. 

	“This brings back the sense of exploration. I’m very proud it was made in a market that’s increasingly myopic about how it’s done.”

	A Whitefalk Films and Produktion Productions production – sold by French sales company MMM Film Sales – sees Wasikowska as Agata, a Polish-Australian writer who arrives in Sarajevo to write about the war. She wants to speak to the survivors, but they question her motives. Not to mention, weird artworks start to mysteriously disappear from the house where she’s staying.

	Dorabialski wanted to combine cinema and literature in the film.
	

	“How do you make these two very different but also very interconnected forms of expression work? Reading is a solitary practice, and we experience cinema collectively,” he states. 

	He was been back and forth about the title pretty much until the premiere in Venice. 

	“And then, suddenly, I felt affection for it. I have a lot of affection also for writers too. The essence of everything I’m interested in is this very particular magic of literature. But where it falls short is silence and stillness. Even a novel that explores silence has to fill that void with language. Cinema has the audience in chains, dictating how long stillness lasts,” he says.

	“I think these two forms complement each other beautifully.”

	Dorabialski comes from the world of video art, where “formal experimentation is not only kind of acceptable – it’s necessary.” 

	“Cinema felt really exciting to me precisely because it has rules. There’s a definite beginning and end time; there’s a dark room and a screen. We’re just brains in a void. I was excited by some of that formal restriction.”

	Wasikowska and Dorabialski both have Polish roots, but in the film, Agata heads to Sarajevo instead.

	“I was interested in the idea of Slavic identity outside Eastern Europe and what it means to be part of this linguistic ethnic group,” he explains. 

	“Much of my work has examined historical similarities throughout Eastern Europe, politically and linguistically. Bosnia and Poland are about as far apart as two Slavic cultures could be, but the concept of Eastern Europe is formed from outside that territory. It’s always the West and the Anglophone world looking at this region and othering this group. I guess I’m playing the insider-outsider game here.”

	He knew that Wasikowska would be the right Agata. 

	“Partly it’s because she has this Polish-Australian connection, but primarily because of the way she chooses and approaches her roles. I knew she could handle the challenge of playing someone who’s very pensive, restrained, quiet and detached.”

	He adds: “Even in the final act of the film, where there’s nothing but Mia’s face, we’re still listening to the story and engaging with its content. Every time I watch it, I notice all the small decisions she made that give depth to her expressions.” 
	

	Wasikowska hasn’t really explored her roots before. Edward Zwick’s “Defiance,” about a Jewish underground resistance movement, came the closest. 

	“I haven’t had the opportunity to do that too much. But just from growing up, it’s very familiar to me,” she says. 

	“My mum and grandma were immigrants, and I observed their experience of trying to find belonging while being nostalgic about Poland. I’ve also traveled back to Poland many times. I connected with that in the script, and with Kuba. I understood the search for belonging and the feeling of being in between cultures even when somewhere feels familiar.”

	That’s Agata’s struggle as well, as she’s desperately trying to figure out how to write about a conflict she hasn’t experienced. And whether it even makes sense. 

	“To me, what’s meaningful is the intention of trying to understand other people and things we haven’t lived through. That’s what it means to be human. It’s our responsibility to try to understand each other,” says Wasikowska. 

	And, according to Dorabialski, artists have a responsibility to respond to the world in which they live. 

	“It’s not like you go to church and all your sins are forgiven just because you’ve made an artwork about Gaza. But shouldn’t we expect art to create change? I’m not convinced that it does, especially in any kind of lasting, meaningful way. But artists have to do it anyway.”

schema.headline: Mia Wasikowska Fills Out the Screen As ‘Agata the Writer’ in Kuba Dorabialski’s Venice Drama: ‘It’s Our Responsibility to Understand Each Other’

title: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’
description: Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.
body:
Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.

	Terry Gilliam, who worked with Thomas on “Tideland” and “The Man Who Killed Don Quixote,” told Variety, “Jeremy Thomas loved making movies. He loved every aspect of the business, but most of all he loved directors. The list of those he worked with is almost endless and I was one of the lucky ones. His taste in filmmaking spanned the globe. He was fearless in getting some very unlikely films financed and released, often to worldwide success. The list is remarkable in range and absolutely unforgettable in quality. Most of all, he was a joy to work with. As your producer you always felt protected and encouraged, rare qualities to experience, especially when lack of time and money are swirling around you, raging at your head. Filmmaking is not cheap and the pressures are intense but Jeremy always remained calm and supportive. He was a rare and very unique gem in the world of producers.”
	

	Luca Guadagnino, who recently put Thomas on camera for his Venice-bowing documentary “Joie De Vivre” to talk about Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci (with whom he made five films), offered Variety a statement about the producer.


	“Jeremy Thomas’ death leaves a gigantic void. The space he was fulfilling was a space of pure cinema. Someone who knew how to collaborate with filmmakers and make them better, and how to be himself — a great filmmaker,” he said. “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci. He was a generous man. He was a kind man. He was a man full of stories to tell, but at the same time, very curious to hear others people’s stories. I regret not having been able, in my life, to be produced by the great Jeremy Thomas, and I say a very moved goodbye to him.”
	

	Thomas was greatly admired and loved by fellow British producers, such as Danny Boyle’s producing partner Andrew Macdonald. Macdonald told Variety that “Jeremy and I bonded over his father [director Ralph Thomas] and my grandfather both producing films for Rank in the 1950s. He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Macdonald’s grandfather was Emeric Pressburger, the co-writer, co-director and producer of “The Red Shoes” and “Black Narcissus,” among other classics.

	Producer Stephen Woolley, whose credits include Oscar-nominated films like “The Crying Game” and “Carol,” told Variety that Thomas was a “colossus.”

	Woolley said, “I first met the maverick and international producer in Tokyo at a buyers’ screening of his movie ‘Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.’ Jeremy Thomas was the person in 1981 in Japan who didn’t suggest but insisted that I be a film producer!!!! He was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and necessary rebel in our industry… he sided with the subversives and movie anarchists and we loved him dearly… and I have to thank him for my career following in similar footsteps avoiding nationalistic stereotypes and embracing the world of cinema.

	“As a distributor, I released most of his eighties films including Oshima’s ‘Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence,’ Frears’ ‘The Hit,’ Roeg’s ‘Insignificance,’ Bertolucci’s ‘Sheltering Sky’ etc., and before that I wrote as a film pundit the cover article for the Sex Pistols movie ‘Rock n Roll Swindle’ for Time Out ( a movie I adored), which he produced with Julien Temple directing. All inspiring!!!

	“And his company HanWay sold a lot of our productions including ‘Made in Dagenham’ and ‘Carol.’ He wasn’t just the Oscar winner of ‘Last Emperor’ (with an Italian director and Irish star set in China!) he was much, much more.

	“Without Jeremy (and a little help from John Boorman) I would never have had the nerve at 27 to make ‘The Company of Wolves’ with the Irish director-writer Neil Jordan and the iconic feminist and anarchic writer Angela Carter. Jeremy showed with his first movie success ‘The Shout’ (with Polish friend and collaborator Skolimowski) that boundaries were there to be ignored or broken. And that movies are an international and all-embracing experience.
	

	“Myself and my producing partner Elizabeth Karlsen look up to his guiding star still moving across the galaxy and inspiring filmmakers from all nations and genders with his extraordinary body of stellar work. Hoping to take guidance from a groundbreaking guru whose love of world cinema defied any easy categorization.”

	Producer and publisher Charles Finch said, “He made great movies and was a loyal, dear friend. His father, Ralph, made a film with my father, Peter, called ‘No Love for Johnnie.’ We spent plenty of time talking movies, cars and praising the devilled kidneys as Wilton’s.”

	On social media, Edinburgh Film Festival CEO and director Paul Ridd said that the “loss of Jeremy Thomas is enormous, to film culture and to the world,” adding that he was “such a beautiful man and a extraordinarily generous supporter” of the festival. 

	Adrian Wootton, chief executive of Film London and the British Film Commission, said that Thomas’ passing was, “Such terribly sad news for Jeremy’s loved ones, family, friends, colleagues, the filmmakers and for the British Film Industry he did so much for.”

	Across a career spanning more than half a century, Thomas produced 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process. In 1988 he won the best picture Oscar for Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor.”

schema.headline: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’

title: Andrew Scott Gets Candid at TIFF About ‘Elsinore’ and People Against Gay Actors Playing Straight Roles: ‘That’s Just Prejudice’
description:
Could Andrew Scott make history?

	That is the big question concerning the Irish actor’s towering performance in “Elsinore,” which debuted in Tellur
body:
Could Andrew Scott make history?

	That is the big question concerning the Irish actor’s towering performance in “Elsinore,” which debuted in Telluride before playing the Toronto International Film Festival. Directed by Simon Stone, the film features Scott as Ian Charleson, a Scottish actor whose career has slowed down since featuring in “Chariots of Fire.” The year is 1989, and when Daniel Day-Lewis walks offstage during a production of “Hamlet” at London’s National Theater, Charleson sees it as an opportunity to show the world what he’s made of as an actor — even as his body is being ravaged by AIDS, and against the advice of his doctor (Olivia Colman), who warns him that the stress could further worsen his health.
	

	As Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote, “The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. ‘Elsinore’ is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first.”


	Scott was widely seen as “snubbed” for his embodiment of Richard Rodgers in “Blue Moon” and the haunted Adam in “All of Us Strangers.”

	On Saturday, Sept. 12, Scott took the stage at the Royal Alexandra Theatre to roaring applause as part of TIFF’s “In Conversation” series to discuss his much-heralded turn in “Elsinore” and his storied career. The talk was moderated by Keith Bennie, TIFF’s vice president of public programming.
	

	The talk began with Bennie asking Scott, 49, who was sporting a striking purple jumper, about the internet’s obsession with him.

	“I don’t have the internet. I never see it,” he joked, before adding, “It’s actually wild: You never know what feral things people [will say].”

	“Elsinore” is the first film Scott has ever produced, so he said it “took a huge amount of encouragement and support and vision from so many people” to bring it to fruition. It was also a very personal project for Scott, who is openly gay and has been acting in theater since the ‘90s, including his aforementioned turn as Hamlet in 2017.

	“You go through stages with it, and the film is so incredibly personal for me, which is the reason why I chose to produce this one,” he explained. “It’s set in the theater and about the representation of gay actors in the ‘90s, and it’s about family. So many things that I really relate to.”

	Scott made his acting debut as a teenager in “Korea,” an Irish film that premiered at TIFF in 1995. And it was a formative experience for him, since he was given a crash course in how to conduct himself on a film set by watching his co-star, screen veteran Donal Donnelly, who led with authority but treated people with dignity and respect.

	“Depressing. No, it was extraordinary. I was 17, and it was the first film I’d ever made,” offered Scott. “I learned how to be on a set because [Donnelly] was incredibly kind and fun with everybody… He wasn’t in any way cruel or anything like that.”

	When Scott was a child, he had a speech impediment, which, in a roundabout way, is how he “fell in love with acting.”

	“When I was a kid, I had a speech impediment — I had a very strong sort of lisp— so I had to go to elocution lessons at seven or eight,” he shared. “It had a drama section to it where you could improvise in front of the other kids.” Performing poetry and monologues in front of a crowd, however small, “amplified something that was dormant” in him.

	At one point during the talk, Bennie shared a scene of Scott’s priest acting alongside Phoebe Waller-Bridge in the second season of “Fleabag,” which became an internet sensation and earned his character the nickname “The Hot Priest.”
	

	“If you had got a script that said, ‘The Hot Priest,’ you’d be like, ‘This is dodgy,’” joked Scott. “It was just called ‘The Priest’ and then the internet took over.”

	Scott, however, was immensely proud of “The Hot Priest” craze in the sense that it helped ease some of his own anxieties about whether the audience would accept a gay actor in a role as a woman’s love interest.

	“I guess there was a fear that I wouldn’t be able to get cast in those roles. That’s what everybody said,” he confessed. “But I knew, because when I did plays, that the people that were waiting at the stage door, they knew my sexuality and they did not care.”

	He continued: “I feel very proud that that was quite a big moment because people were like, ‘The actor is gay. Whoa!’ And it is like this idea that the audience is stupid. We go to see ‘Batman,’ and it’s like, ‘Oh my god! He is not a bat?’”

	And if you don’t like Scott in those types of roles, that’s on you.

	“That’s just prejudice,” said Scott. “And we won’t cater to those people, or I’m certainly not going to.”

	About an hour in, the talk swung back to “Elsinore,” a film — and performance — that people will be talking about throughout awards season.

	“It’s about how we use our time, and he was enormously fun, attractive, beautiful, amazingly gifted actor,” Scott said of playing Charleson. “And the film is about the support that he got and the courage that he displayed. The reason I was so attracted to it, I think, is because it doesn’t end well for any of us, and quality of time is what he chose… I know what an Olympian, absolutely exhausting task that is [to play Hamlet]. I did it 150 times… The idea that he did it when he was so unwell, it always just gets me.”

	Scott, who got choked up while discussing the film, also lamented how difficult it was for Charleson to act, or even exist, at a time when gay men, particularly those with HIV/AIDS, were being viciously discriminated against.

	“There weren’t any gay actors — for no reason,” he remarked. “That was taken away from them.”

schema.headline: Andrew Scott Gets Candid at TIFF About ‘Elsinore’ and People Against Gay Actors Playing Straight Roles: ‘That’s Just Prejudice’

title: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country’ Wins Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Belarusian director Andrei Kutsila’s “Letters from the Silenced Country,” a portrayal of contemporary Belarus seen through the lives of five individ
body:
Belarusian director Andrei Kutsila’s “Letters from the Silenced Country,” a portrayal of contemporary Belarus seen through the lives of five individuals whose existence has been upended by state violence and political repression, is the winner of The Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary awarded in partnership with Artemis Rising Foundation at the Venice Film Festival.

	The juried prize, which honors a documentary filmmaker with a feature in the 2026 Venice official selection that calls attention to a key social issue with journalistic and creative prowess, is presented at the fest as a collateral impact award.
	

	Built around personal letters written from prison, exile, and underground life, “Letters from the Silenced Country” – which premiered at Venice out-of-competition – combines observational documentary, archival footage, and animation based on drawings created in confinement. “Rather than a broad political overview, the film focuses on individual stories, of protest, imprisonment, escape, and everyday resistance, told through the people living them,” according to a provided synopsis.


	The Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Award’s jury at Venice comprised Filipino-American star Liza Soberano; Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne; Oscar-winning producer and founder of Artemis Rising Foundation Regina K. Scully; Oscar-winning producer and co-founder of Impact Partners Geralyn White Dreyfous; and founder and CEO of Think-Film Impact Production, Danielle Turkov Wilson.

	“Letters from the Silenced Country puts a human face on a crisis too often reduced to headlines and numbers, illustrating the impossible choices people make to hold on to their humanity,” the jury collectively said in a statement. 
	

	“Though it is rooted in Belarus, its story reaches far beyond one country’s borders, it speaks to anyone who has ever loved someone from a distance, or fought to stay connected to who they are under pressure to disappear,” they added. “The way the director blends letters, drawings, and memory into the storytelling captures not only grief, but love, hope, and tenderness – the full range of what it means to remain human. It’s a powerful example of how a documentary can show how the most personal stories can also be the most universal.”

	The prize carries $10,000 in cash from Artemis Rising Foundation.

	Earlier this year, husband-and-wife filmmaking duo Joshua and Rebecca Tickell were jointly awarded the Golden Globes Prize for Documentary awarded in partnership with Artemis Rising Foundation at Cannes.



	

									Courtesy Think-Film
	



	From left to right: Golden Globes President Helen Hoehne, actress Liza Soberano, Venice Film Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera, Think-Film founder and CEO Danielle Turkov Wilson.

schema.headline: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country’ Wins Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Pierce Brosnan Thinks the Next James Bond Will Be ‘Someone That None of Us Know About’: ‘There Are Lots of Good Hats in the Ring’
description: Ever since Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming James Bond film was announced, the million-dollar question has been: Who will take on the role of the icon
body:
Ever since Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming James Bond film was announced, the million-dollar question has been: Who will take on the role of the iconic spy? Now, former 007 Pierce Brosnan is offering his thoughts. 

	In a recent interview with The Times, the actor, who played the character in four films from 1995 to 2002, said that “there are lots of good hats in the ring” and “lots of great actors” being considered. “I see it. I follow it. They could probably just go left-field and pick someone that none of us know about.”
	

	When it comes to names, Brosnan remained neutral: “I wouldn’t pick anyone,” he continued. “My wife told me not to say anything and I’ve said too much. Because once I say something it goes [everywhere] and I get hanged.”


	Brosnan also explained that he hasn’t revisited his own Bond films since their release. “I have no desire to see myself in Bond,” he said. “I’m just a member of the audience now awaiting the next Bond and wishing him well.”  

	This isn’t the first time the actor has waded into the Bond waters — back in Aug. 2025, while speaking with the Radio Times, Brosnan joked that he’d return as a senior citizen Bond. 

	“I don’t think anyone wants to see a craggy, 72-year-old Bond, but if Villeneuve had something up his sleeve I would look at it in a heartbeat,” Brosnan said. “Why not? It’s great entertainment. It could be lots of laughs. Bald caps, prosthetics… who knows?”

	Variety previously reported that Amazon MGM Studios enlisted casting director Nina Gold to find the new secret agent. Her credits include the Netflix series “The Crown,” five films in the Star Wars franchise, “Les Misérables,” “The Martian” and “Conclave.” In 2025, she was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Hamnet.” 
	

	While the final casting for the film has not been confirmed, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and Jack Lowden have all been reported as among those in the final running.

schema.headline: Pierce Brosnan Thinks the Next James Bond Will Be ‘Someone That None of Us Know About’: ‘There Are Lots of Good Hats in the Ring’

title: Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Venice Jury Didn’t Award ‘Woman Unknown’ the Golden Lion Just Because It Was Directed by a Woman: It ‘Was Like a Laser Beam’
description: Maggie Gyllenhaal kicked off her term as Venice jury president by calling out the lack of women filmmakers in the running for the prestigious Golden
body:
Maggie Gyllenhaal kicked off her term as Venice jury president by calling out the lack of women filmmakers in the running for the prestigious Golden Lion. And on Saturday night, she concluded it by awarding the prize to the only film solely directed by a woman: May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown.”

	But at a press conference after the awards ceremony, Gyllenhaal rejected the notion that she and her fellow jury members were making any sort of “political statement,” as one journalist put it, with their selection. “I actually didn’t see ‘Woman Unknown,'” she deadpanned. “I just was like, ‘It’s made by a woman and so, Golden Lion!'”
	

	Speaking sincerely, Gyllenhaal continued: “I will say that, of course, I anticipated that question. There are many movies that women made that I don’t like and some that I actively, strongly don’t like, just like films made by men. I have one vote just as each member of this jury does, and so all of the decisions that we make are always complicated, always involve a lot of conversation.”


	She sighed and added, “I think I’m tired of talking about this same subject over and over. I will continue to do it, but just for a minute, here in this incredible place, I just want to celebrate a beautifully made movie that I felt was like a laser beam just for the well-made movie that it is.”

	Gyllenhaal’s jury also consisted of “The Voice of Hind Rajab” director Kaouther Ben Hania, Hong Kong filmmaking giant Johnnie To, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat, French director and screenwriter Xavier Giannoli, “The Brutalist” composer Daniel Blumberg and U.S.-based Italian film academic Francesco Casetti.
	

	She also explained the jury’s decision to award “Woman Unknown” star Mathilde Arcel with the Volpi Cup for best actress. “You’re allowed to give two awards to a Golden Lion winner if the second award you want to give is unanimous,” Gyllenhaal said. “So we unanimously allowed to award Mathilde, who I’d like to say publicly, for all the press, is going to blow our socks off.”

	The only other movie in competition involving a woman director was “NAZA,” which was co-helmed by Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham. The powerful documentary about the conflict in Gaza took home the special jury prize. 

	Asked about it during the press conference, Gyllenhaal said she admired the film’s “immense bravery and intelligence.” She added that her fellow juror Ben Hania helped illuminate her to the fact that “the way in which it’s shot and put together is about systems.”

	“I know Jonathan Glazer, who made ‘Zone of Interest,’ was one of the producers  — it reminded me a little bit of ‘Zone of Interest’ in that way, which is also about systems,” she continued. “And one of the things that I loved about the film was the way that it non-literally expressed that.”

	See the full list of Venice award winners here.

schema.headline: Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Venice Jury Didn’t Award ‘Woman Unknown’ the Golden Lion Just Because It Was Directed by a Woman: It ‘Was Like a Laser Beam’

title: Woman Dead After Undergoing 6 Cosmetic Procedures at Once
description:
Brazilian Woman
                          Dead After 8-Hour Surgery, 6 Cosmetic Procedures At Onc
body:
Brazilian Woman
                          Dead After 8-Hour Surgery, 6 Cosmetic Procedures At Once
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 12, 2026
                            7:23 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 12, 2026
                                8:15 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A woman who underwent 6 cosmetic procedures at once during a marathon 8-hour procedure has died ... and now the 51-year-old's sister is demanding answers.
      
    
            Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved $118K Brazilian Real -- equivalent to $22,918 USD -- over two years to undergo the plastic surgery -- which involved a facelift, blepharoplasty, liposuction and facial fat grafting -- in Goiânia, Brazil.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Andreia, who was living in Spain before the surgery, died in the days after the procedure on August 12 ... G1 reported.
      
    
            Now her sister Djiane Vieira is saying Andreia -- whose dream was to have this surgery -- did not have a pre-procedure consultation ... and that her pre-op tests were done in Spain, not Brazil.
      

            Djiane says that after Andreia's tongue started swelling severely, she tried reaching out to the doctor's medical team ... but her sister says didn't receive the proper care before it was too late.
      
    
            She told G1 ... "My sister is dying. For God’s sake. You answer the phone, but nobody shows up. For God’s sake."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She claims that the local Ankar Hospital did not have an ICU or an emergency ambulance.
      
    
            According to Djiane ... Andreia died in her arms after multiple resuscitation attempts were made.
      
    
            Dr. Lessandro Martins said in a legal statement ... "Out of respect for medical confidentiality — which persists even after death, as mandated by the Medical Code of Ethics — no interviews will be granted, nor will comments be made regarding clinical data... The doctor trusts that the investigation will demonstrate the correctness of the care provided."
      
    
            Meanwhile, a lawyer representing Ankar Hospital says Andreia "received immediate emergency care" and "necessary measures were taken" to treat her.

title: Scooter Braun Shares PDA-Filled Birthday Post For Sydney Sweeney

body:
Sydney Sweeney
                          BF Scooter Dips Her in Front of Palace For Bday ...
                          I Love You, Syd!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 12, 2026
                            12:11 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Scooter Braun is dancing with, dipping, and makin' out with Sydney Sweeney in his PDA-filled birthday post dedicated to his girlfriend's big day ... and his note to her is even sweeter.
      
    
            Filming in front of what appears to be Avignon's Palace of the Popes in the South of France ... the music mogul and "Euphoria" actress -- who turns 29 today -- danced to Mitski's "My Love Mine All Mine" in his Instagram post that he uploaded Saturday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Scooter wrote in the caption ... "You make me smile harder, laugh louder, adventure more, and dream bigger. You’ve made the ordinary feel exciting and the future feel like something I can’t wait to get to."
      
    
            Adding that her "giggle can change an entire day" ... Scooter admitted he loves "how corny we can be together, because nothing else matters. There are a million things I could say, but the ones that matter most are just for you." And yes, he even used the L-word!!! 👀
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            His sweet birthday message comes as the couple seemingly have gotten even more serious ... as we reported, Sydney has been spending more time with Scooter's kids in recent weeks.
      
    
            The two also jetted off to Venice to flaunt their amore last week ... taking a boat ride down the canal together.
      
    
            Happy birthday, Syd! We hope it's a euphoric one.
